concept_html:
Named entity recognition (NER) labels every word. The usual scheme is BIO: B- begins an entity, I- continues it, and O is outside any entity. "Ana visited New York" is B-PER O B-LOC I-LOC. On open survey answers, NER finds brands, products and places.

The labels belong to words, but the model sees subword tokens. A BERT tokenizer splits "staffs" into staff and ##s, and adds [CLS] and [SEP]. Pass the words already split, and ask which word each token came from (transformers 5.22):

enc = tokenizer(["Ana", "visited", "London", "staffs"], is_split_into_words=True)
enc.word_ids()     # [None, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3, None]

None marks a special token. A repeated ID marks a word split into several tokens. Align the word labels to tokens with three rules:

  • a special token gets -100;
  • the first token of a word gets the word's label;
  • any later token of the same word gets -100.

-100 is the default ignore_index of nn.CrossEntropyLoss in PyTorch 2.15, and the Hugging Face token-classification loss uses it. Those positions add nothing to the loss, so each word counts once, whatever its number of pieces.

AutoModelForTokenClassification.from_pretrained(name, num_labels=len(tags), id2label=..., label2id=...) returns logits of shape (batch, tokens, num_labels). To predict, take the argmax per token, then read each word's label from its first token. The load report lists the pooler weights as UNEXPECTED. That is fine: a token head does not use the pooler.

Check alignment on a real example before training. Labels shifted by one position still train, and the loss still falls, but the model learns to tag the word next to each entity.

lines: IGNORE = -100
def align_labels(word_ids: list[int | None], word_labels: list[int]) -> list[int]:
"""Token labels from word labels: first token of each word only.
Args:
word_ids: From enc.word_ids(): the word index of each token, None for special tokens.
word_labels: One label ID per word.
Returns:
One label per token, IGNORE for special tokens and later pieces of a word.
Raises:
ValueError: If a word index has no label.
"""
aligned: list[int] = []
previous: int | None = None
for word_id in word_ids:
if word_id is None:
aligned.append(IGNORE)
elif word_id != previous:
if word_id >= len(word_labels):
raise ValueError(f"word {word_id} has no label; got {len(word_labels)} labels")
aligned.append(word_labels[word_id])
else:
aligned.append(IGNORE)
previous = word_id
return aligned
def encode_example(tokenizer, words: list[str], tags: list[str], label2id: dict[str, int]) -> dict[str, list[int]]:
"""Token IDs, attention mask and aligned labels for one sentence."""
enc = tokenizer(words, is_split_into_words=True, truncation=True)
labels = align_labels(enc.word_ids(), [label2id[t] for t in tags])
return {"input_ids": enc["input_ids"], "attention_mask": enc["attention_mask"], "labels": labels}

def align_labels(word_ids: list[int | None], word_labels: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """Token labels from word labels, first token of each word only.

    Args:
        word_ids: Word index per token, None for special tokens.
        word_labels: One label ID per word.

    Returns:
        One label per token, -100 where the loss should ignore it.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If a word index has no label.
    """
    aligned: list[int] = []
    previous: int | None = None
    for word_id in word_ids:
        if word_id is None:
            aligned.append(-100)
        elif word_id != previous:
            if word_id >= len(word_labels):
                raise ValueError(f"word {word_id} has no label")
            aligned.append(word_labels[word_id])
        else:
            aligned.append(-100)
        previous = word_id
    return aligned

Write word_predictions(word_ids, token_preds) -> list[int]: one predicted label per word, read from each word's first token.

  • token_preds holds one predicted label per token, aligned with word_ids.
  • Skip None positions. Return the predictions in word order.
  • Raise ValueError if the two lists differ in length.
exercises.solution:
def word_predictions(word_ids: list[int | None], token_preds: list[int]) -> list[int]:
    """One label per word, from the word's first token.

    Args:
        word_ids: Word index per token, None for special tokens.
        token_preds: Predicted label per token.

    Returns:
        Predicted labels in word order.

    Raises:
        ValueError: If the lists differ in length.
    """
    if len(word_ids) != len(token_preds):
        raise ValueError(f"{len(word_ids)} word IDs but {len(token_preds)} predictions")
    preds: list[int] = []
    previous: int | None = None
    for word_id, pred in zip(word_ids, token_preds):
        if word_id is not None and word_id != previous:
            preds.append(pred)
        previous = word_id
    return preds

title: Token classification, named entities and subword labels
why_html: A team trained a model to find product names in open answers. Validation F1 looked fine on short answers and collapsed on answers with brand names such as "SuperSaver". Their alignment gave the word's label to every token by position in the word list, so after the first split word, every label slid one or more tokens to the right. Aligning with word_ids() fixed it.
